_meta.article_title: Keep Strengthening Your Friendship With Your Mate
_meta.preparation_standard: Hand-drafted in-chat by Fable 5. Single-brother-authentic: ¶3-9 firsthand (choosing a mate), ¶10-17 from observation. Brother-in-seat voice per audience_critic doctrine.

notes.content: You know what got me about Proverbs 27:9? We usually think the friends who make our heart rejoice are the ones who agree with us — the ones who make us feel good in the moment. But the verse ties the sweetness to something else. The paragraph says good friends "give us honest advice when we need it" — and that's the part we don't put on the gift list. James 1:17 says every good gift is from above, and when I count the friends Jehovah has given me, the ones I'm most grateful for aren't the ones who co-signed everything I wanted to do. It's the ones who loved me enough to tell me the truth when I didn't want it. That's the gift part. Anybody can find somebody to agree with them. But a friend who loves God first, and loves you enough to be honest — you can't buy that. Jehovah has to give it.

underlines.phrase: They share in our joy when we are happy, comfort us when we feel down, and give us honest advice when we need it
make the heart rejoice

notes.content: What hit me about Matthew 19:6 is the word Jesus picked — "what God has yoked together." A yoke isn't a weld. A weld holds two pieces of metal by itself; you can walk away and it stays fused. A yoke joins two who still have to walk — together, in step, pulling the same direction, every single day. So when the paragraph says a couple "cannot take their friendship for granted," that's not a warning stuck onto the verse. It's in the verse. Jehovah did the yoking; the walking in step is what the couple keeps doing. And I love the honesty here — neglect it and the same house can hold two lonely people. Nurture it and it's the closest bond two humans can have. Same yoke either way. The difference is whether they keep walking together in it.

underlines.phrase: they need to keep working at strengthening it
they can enjoy the closest bond that two humans could ever have

notes.content: I'll be honest — this paragraph checked me as a single brother. Because I'll spend an hour reading reviews before I buy a pair of shoes. Forty dollars, and I want to know what a thousand strangers think first. Then I'll check three websites before I pick a phone plan. And the paragraph is asking — do we bring even that much care to the decisions that actually shape a life? It says big decisions "can affect our life for a long time," and marriage is about as long as it gets on this side of the new world. So the counsel to think about risks, benefits, and outcomes isn't cold or unromantic. It's the opposite. The things we research carefully are the things we take seriously. If I'd research a pair of shoes I'll wear for a year, how much more a friendship I'm choosing for life?

underlines.phrase: Big decisions can affect our life for a long time, so it is important to consider them carefully

notes.content: The phrase in Proverbs 18:22 that I never noticed before is the second half. "The one who finds a good wife has found something good" — that part we know. But then — "he receives goodwill from Jehovah." From Jehovah. Meaning when somebody chooses a mate Jehovah's way, Jehovah doesn't just watch it happen and nod. He responds. There's goodwill flowing back from him toward that marriage. So choosing a mate by God's standards was never just a decision between two people — it's a decision Jehovah personally answers. And Isaiah 48:17 makes sense of why: he's "the One teaching you to benefit yourself." Every standard he sets around marriage is him trying to hand us the good outcome. So for those of us who are single, looking to Jehovah for guidance isn't a restriction on the choice. It's the part of the choice where Jehovah gets to give something back.

underlines.phrase: it makes sense to look to him for guidance when choosing a mate
Jehovah always knows what is best for us

notes.content: Psalm 25:14 says close friendship with Jehovah belongs to those who fear him — and the paragraph starts there on purpose. When we got baptized, we became friends of God. So when it says choose your mate "from among Jehovah's friends," I had to sit with what that actually means. You're not picking from strangers. You're picking from your best Friend's circle. And that reframes the whole thing — because when I've reasoned like the paragraph warns against, like maybe options are limited, or maybe the person would come into the truth later — what I'd really be saying is that my Friend's circle isn't good enough, and I know better than he does who belongs in my life. First Corinthians 7:39 says "only in the Lord," and it reads like a restriction until you see it from the friendship side. Jehovah isn't fencing us in. He's introducing us.

underlines.phrase: you should choose your prospective mate from among Jehovah’s friends
unevenly yoked

notes.content: You know what I noticed about the questions in this paragraph? Not one of them can be answered in an interview. 'How does he treat his family? How does he handle disagreements? What's his attitude toward money?' — you can't ask those across a dinner table and trust the answer, because anybody can interview well. Jobs figured this out a long time ago — that's why there's a probation period after the interview. The résumé says one thing; six months on the job tells the truth. And that's really what the paragraph means by looking at somebody objectively. Not suspiciously — objectively. Watching how he treats his mother when he's tired. How he acts when the disagreement is real and nobody's performing. Time and observation are how the truth comes out, and that's not being unloving toward the person. It's being honest about how much a marriage weighs.

underlines.phrase: not just any baptized person is a suitable mate
How does he handle disagreements?

notes.content: There's one question in this paragraph that stood out to me above the others: "Will he help me to keep serving Jehovah more fully?" That's a different kind of measurement. Because most of the courtship questions look at the other person — their qualities, their habits, their love for Jehovah. But this one looks at what happens to you around them. Colossians 3 talks about "the new personality," and here's the thing — you can see somebody's new personality most clearly in what it does to yours. Around the right person, your service gets bigger. Your prayers get more honest. Your meetings attendance doesn't have to fight against the relationship — the relationship carries it. And around the wrong person, even a baptized wrong person, everything spiritual in your life quietly shrinks. So the question isn't just 'do they love Jehovah.' It's 'does my love for Jehovah grow or shrink in their presence.' That answer takes time, which is exactly what courtship is for.

underlines.phrase: use your courtship to get to know your prospective mate well
Do we share the same spiritual goals?

notes.content: What Sarah did in this paragraph is really striking when you count it up — she asked the flatmate, the pioneer partner, an elder, mutual friends, and the sisters in his congregation. Five different angles on one brother. And here's why that works: a person can perform for one audience, but nobody can perform for every audience at the same time. The flatmate sees him when he's tired. The pioneer partner sees him when the ministry is slow. The sisters see how he treats women he's not trying to impress. Reputation is just the word for what you're like when each audience compares notes — and it's the one thing that can't be faked in every direction at once. So asking around isn't gossip and it isn't distrust. It's humility. It's admitting that the person I'm looking at through interested eyes might look different through honest ones — and wanting the truth more than the feeling.

underlines.phrase: try to discern what the person is really like
Find out how others view your friend

notes.content: This half of the paragraph is short but it might be the heaviest sentence in the whole article — don't ignore nagging doubts or the honest observations of mature friends. Because the moment those doubts show up is exactly the moment we're least equipped to weigh them. There's a reason the paragraph pairs the two together — your own nagging doubt and your mature friends' observations. They're the same signal coming through two different receivers. The doubt is what you noticed but don't want to see. The friend's observation is what they noticed and don't want to say. And when both are pointing the same direction — that's not an attack on the relationship. That's Jehovah's provision of 'a multitude of counselors' doing exactly what Proverbs said it would do. Ending a courtship feels like a failure in the moment. But it's not a failure. It's the system working before the vows instead of after them.

underlines.phrase: Do not ignore nagging doubts you might have or honest observations that mature friends make

notes.content: Watching the strongest marriages in my family, I've noticed something about this paragraph — the list it gives is so ordinary. Talk about everyday happenings. Share thoughts and feelings. Show affection. Have fun together. There's nothing dramatic on that list. And that's the point I had to learn by watching, because from the outside you'd think strong marriages are built on the big things — the anniversaries, the vacations, the crisis they survived. But the couples I most want to imitate are the ones who like each other on a random Tuesday. The ones still talking in the car. Still laughing at the kitchen table long after the food is done. The friendship is made out of small time, in volume, and it can't be replaced by big occasions any more than one feast a year can replace daily bread. Busy is real — the paragraph doesn't pretend otherwise. But no matter how busy, the time is the friendship.

underlines.phrase: keep their friendship and marriage strong by making time for each other

notes.content: This paragraph is careful and I want to be careful with it too. It's talking about brothers and sisters who took work far from home — and let's be honest about why people do that: love. Providing is love; that's what makes this hard. But the paragraph does the math out loud. There may be some financial advantages — it grants that — and then, a prolonged absence can be disastrous for a marriage. And I think about 1 Timothy 5:8, providing for your household — a household isn't just fed with money. It's fed with presence. If the check goes home but the friendship starves, the provision is incomplete in the way that matters most. Nobody sitting here should feel condemned by that — circumstances get complicated and mercy belongs in this conversation. But for those of us still making these decisions, it's worth weighing what the extra income buys against what the distance spends.

underlines.phrase: a prolonged absence can be disastrous for a marriage
away from their family for an extended period

notes.content: The cross-reference in this paragraph is the quiet gem — the article says compare Amos 3:3, and in our Bible that verse reads, "Will two walk together unless they have met by appointment?" By appointment. I always heard that verse as just 'people need to agree.' But the word picture is two people who scheduled it. Nobody ends up walking together by accident — not in Amos, and according to Roxanne in this paragraph, not in marriage either. She said they came to see the need to schedule time together just like other important events, and at first that sounds unromantic, right? Putting your own wife on the calendar. But look what actually gets scheduled in our lives: meetings, assignments, the ministry — the things we refuse to leave to chance. What gets penciled in whenever — that's what quietly disappears. So the calendar isn't the death of the romance. The calendar is the proof of it.

underlines.phrase: the need to schedule time together
We sometimes put our phones away

notes.content: Myriam said something in this paragraph that stayed with me — she loves praying together with her husband because she hears "the depth of my husband's love for Jehovah." Think about what's actually happening in that moment. She isn't just spending time with her mate. She's listening in on her mate's friendship with Jehovah. That's a side of a person nobody else ever gets to see — not their friends, not the congregation, just the one kneeling next to them. And Proverbs 27:17 says iron sharpens iron, one friend sharpens another — but sharpening needs contact, and spiritual things together is where that contact happens. The Bible reading, the ministry, the prayer. A couple can watch shows together every night and still be spiritually strangers. But the couple that prays together has heard each other's deepest friendship out loud. That's why the paragraph says above all. Everything else is time together. This is the three of you together.

underlines.phrase: spend time together in spiritual activities
I cherish these moments

notes.content: I'm grateful the Bible talks the way this paragraph shows. First Corinthians 7:28 tells people considering marriage that they "will have tribulation in their flesh." Will. Not might. And the study note says that just means the ordinary problems common to married couples. Now think about how the world talks to engaged couples — everything is soulmates and fairy tales, and then reality arrives and people conclude they must have married the wrong person, because it wasn't supposed to be hard. Paul does the opposite. He hands you the cost before you sign. And that's not pessimism — that's the same reason we trust Jehovah about everything else. A friend who tells you the road has potholes before you drive it isn't discouraging you from the trip. He's making sure the first pothole doesn't convince you the whole road was a mistake. The tribulation is normal. The couple that knows that keeps driving.

underlines.phrase: married couples will experience challenges in their marriage
will have tribulation in their flesh

notes.content: When Notre-Dame caught fire a few years back, I don't remember one person saying tear it down. The roof was gone, the spire collapsed — and the whole world said restore it. It took five years and hundreds of millions, and nobody called that wasteful, because the building was precious. That's exactly the illustration this paragraph is making. All marriages are precious — and just as a damaged work of art can be repaired, a troubled marriage can be saved. What gets me is what the restoration decision reveals: nobody looked at the damage to decide the building's worth. They looked at the worth to decide what the damage deserved. Malachi 2:16 tells us how Jehovah feels about divorce, so when a couple does the slow, expensive work of restoring instead of walking away, they're saying about their marriage what the world said about that cathedral — the damage is real, but it doesn't get the last word.

underlines.phrase: a troubled marriage can be saved
all marriages are precious

notes.content: There's a phrase in 1 Corinthians 13:5 that reads like bookkeeping — love "does not keep account of the injury." Keep account. That's ledger language. And I had to admit how natural the ledger is when you're hurt — every offense gets itemized, dated, filed, ready to be pulled out in the next disagreement as evidence. The verse doesn't say the injury didn't happen. It says love doesn't post it to the books. And that connects to the line in this paragraph I can't shake: rather than look for a way out, look for a way back into each other's heart. A way out and a way back both take work — the difference is what the work is for. Then Ecclesiastes 4:12 explains why the way back is even possible: the threefold cord. Two strands under strain can fray. But when Jehovah is the third strand — the strongest one — the rope holds while the other two heal.

underlines.phrase: do your best to look for a way back into each other’s heart
the third and strongest strand

notes.content: It matters to me which book this last verse comes from. "Enjoy life with your beloved wife" — that's Ecclesiastes 9:9. Ecclesiastes — the book that calls everything vanity, vapor, chasing the wind. Solomon looks at wealth, vapor. Fame, vapor. Pleasure, houses, achievements — vapor, all of it. And then the same book, the same pen, stops and says: enjoy life with your beloved wife. The one book most qualified to call marriage meaningless is the book that tells you it isn't. So whether we're single and choosing carefully, or married and strengthening what we have, this is what Jehovah wanted the whole article to leave us with — he wants his servants happy. Not enduring marriage. Enjoying it. In a world where almost everything really is vapor, Jehovah put a few solid things in our hands, and a mate who's your best friend is one of them. That's worth choosing carefully. And it's worth keeping strong.

underlines.phrase: choose your lifelong friend carefully
continue strengthening your friendship with your mate
Jehovah wants all his servants to be happy
